notes: Complete reserved judgment on police injury pension degree assessment.

enrichment.short_title: Police injury award: apportioning disablement to duty injuries only
key_facts: Mr Lewis-Davidson, a former South Wales police officer, retired on medical grounds with depression attributed partly to overwork and partly to stress from child-protection and police investigations and from loss of pay during sickness absence.

Dr Choudhary had certified that his disablement was partly the result of a duty injury, entitling him to an injury award; Dr Morgan, acting as medical referee on appeal over degree of disablement, assessed major disablement (51–75%) by treating all contributing causes as employment-related.
The police authority accepted entitlement to an injury award but contended that only disablement from the overwork duty injury could count when fixing the degree under regulation H1(2)(d).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review by the police authority of a medical referee's decision under the Police Pensions Regulations 1987.
enrichment.outcome: Dr Morgan's decision quashed and the degree-of-disablement issue remitted to a fresh medical referee.
enrichment.ratio: When assessing the degree of disablement for an injury pension under regulation H1(2)(d), only the effect of injuries received in the execution of duty may be counted; where disablement arises from separate duty and non-duty injuries, apportionment is required, and a medical referee who applies an employment-attribution test rather than the regulation A11 duty-injury test errs in law unless that error is irrelevant.
legal_issues: Whether stress from internal police investigations and financial hardship during sickness absence can be treated as injuries received in the execution of duty
Whether Dr Morgan had to consider whether the officer suffered one injury or several when assessing degree of disablement
Whether the police authority was precluded from challenging the medical referee's approach by its earlier acceptance of Dr Choudhary's certificate

enrichment.short_title: 12-year civil proceedings order against habitual vexatious litigant Kevin Mahon
key_facts: The Attorney General applied for a civil proceedings order against Kevin Mahon after he issued at least 31 actions since September 2000, almost all struck out or dismissed.
Mahon's litigation concerned a refused Hackney carriage licence, housing and income support disputes, and a long-running neighbour dispute with Mr and Mrs Rainbow.

In a police interview Mahon admitted using litigation to harass opponents, inflate costs, and pressure neighbours to sell their home; he was later serving a custodial sentence arising from that conduct.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's application under section 42 of the Supreme Court Act 1981 for a civil proceedings order.
enrichment.outcome: Civil proceedings order made for 12 years; application granted.
enrichment.ratio: Where a litigant habitually and persistently institutes hopeless civil proceedings and applications without reasonable ground, section 42 empowers the High Court to make a civil proceedings order; the court may look at the whole litigation history rather than the merits of any single claim, and such orders are compatible with Convention rights.
legal_issues: Whether Mahon's conduct satisfied the statutory test of habitual and persistent vexatious litigation
Whether section 42 is compatible with the European Convention on Human Rights
What period and form of civil proceedings order was appropriate

notes: Complete Court of Appeal lease construction judgment on VAT recovery.

enrichment.short_title: Landlord's late VAT waiver notice did not create retrospective tenant liability
key_facts: Foreign Property APS, successor landlord under a Praed Street lease, elected in May 1999 to waive VAT exemption but did not supply the tenant with the required election documents until over a year later.

The landlord claimed £26,929.54 VAT on rent paid between March 1999 and June 2000; the Secretary of State tenant argued clause 5(10)(i) meant no VAT was payable for that period once documents were supplied late.
The lease also contained outgoings and VAT clauses in clauses 3(2)(A), 3(31) and 5(10).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from the Mayor's and City of London Court to the Court of Appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Read together, clause 5(10)(i) of the lease disapplied section 89 VAT Act 1994 so that, where the landlord failed to supply election and registration documents contemporaneously with notifying HMRC, the tenant was never liable for VAT on rent for the prior period; the 'until' proviso eliminated rather than merely deferred liability.
legal_issues: Whether clause 5(10)(i) postponed or extinguished the tenant's liability for VAT on rent before supply of the required documents
Whether clause 3(31) required VAT to be paid whenever rent was due or only when documents had been supplied
Whether the landlord's construction accorded with business common sense

notes: Complete judgment on section 4 hard-cases support policy and delays.

enrichment.short_title: Home Secretary must reconsider withholding information on section 4 asylum support
key_facts: Two failed asylum seekers, Iraqi Kurd Salih and Iranian Rahmani, sought judicial review of NASS practice of not telling eligible failed asylum seekers about section 4 'hard cases' accommodation support and of delays in providing it.

Standard NASS withdrawal letters ending section 95 support did not mention section 4; Salih waited about eight weeks and Rahmani about three weeks after applying before accommodation was arranged, during which they were destitute.

The Secretary of State's policy treated section 4 support as exceptional, often only after eviction from Part VI accommodation, and relied on advice agencies and lawyers to spread information about the scheme.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review following successful interim relief; permission granted to challenge general NASS practice.
enrichment.outcome: Policy of not informing eligible failed asylum seekers about hard-cases support held unlawful; Secretary of State ordered to reconsider his practice; delay issue not resolved by general declaration.
enrichment.ratio: A public authority's extra-statutory policy governing eligibility for section 4 accommodation must be made known to those who may need it; deliberately withholding information about hard-cases support from apparently eligible failed asylum seekers is inconsistent with constitutional principles of accessibility and irrational, even though Parliament imposed no express duty to notify individuals.
legal_issues: Whether NASS may lawfully refrain from informing failed asylum seekers about section 4 support
Whether eviction from section 95 accommodation is an implicit precondition of section 4 eligibility
Whether administrative delays in providing section 4 support are unlawful

notes: Complete reserved judgment on capitalisation and Form E misconduct.

enrichment.short_title: Capitalisation of long-term maintenance after deliberately false Form E disclosure

statutes_considered.title: Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975

key_facts: W applied to capitalise a joint-lives spousal maintenance order of £27,173 less tax made in 1989 after 21 years of separation; H, a chartered accountant, swore a Form E showing negative net worth by treating £2.5m contingent liabilities as hard debts and omitting substantial assets.
H's true net worth was about £2.7m; W had only her Dorking home worth about £260,000 and significant unpaid costs.
The court found H deliberately misrepresented his finances to resist capitalisation; his former solicitors made unintentional errors that only partly mitigated his conduct.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to vary and capitalise an existing periodical payments order under section 31(7) Matrimonial Causes Act 1973.
enrichment.outcome: Maintenance varied to £34,000 net per annum backdated to 7 December 2001; lump sum of £560,000 plus £12,473 arrears ordered; H ordered to pay £71,100 of W's excess costs on the indemnity basis; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Form E requires honest realistic valuation of assets and liabilities: contingent claims may be narrated but should not be inserted as hard debts unless more likely than not to crystallise; where a payer deliberately falsifies disclosure, the court may capitalise maintenance using a lower Duxbury rate for an elderly vulnerable payee and award indemnity costs for litigation caused by the misconduct.
legal_issues: How to value contingent liabilities and omitted pensions in Form E
The correct Duxbury rate and life expectancy for capitalising joint-lives maintenance
Whether H's former solicitors' errors reduced his culpability or warranted a wasted costs order
Whether the judgment should be anonymised

enrichment.short_title: Tenby harbour byelaws validly used to control Castle Square terrace parking
key_facts: The claimants own No. 3 Castle Square, Tenby, fronting a raised terrace above the harbour; they had controlled parking there with chains and bollards since the 1970s while the council historically did not assert public highway or ownership status.
In 2003 Pembrokeshire County Council made harbour Terms and Directions under 1995 Tenby Harbour byelaws to allocate seven resident parking bays on the terrace and charge £100 per permit.
The council used harbour powers because the roads were unadopted and ownership was uncertain, making Road Traffic Regulation Act controls vulnerable to challenge.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of harbour parking Terms and Directions; amendment allowed to argue ultra vires use of harbour powers.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed with costs; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Harbour byelaw powers may lawfully be used to control parking on land within the defined harbour estate where the council reasonably considers that doing so is necessary to manage harbour access and operations; the claimants could not establish a possession under Article 1 Protocol 1 on the unresolved ownership evidence.
legal_issues: Whether parking control on the raised terrace was within harbour revision order and byelaw powers or an impermissible town-centre traffic scheme
Whether the decision was Wednesbury unreasonable
Whether the Directions infringed Article 1 Protocol 1 ECHR

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment dismissing Gurkha Article 14 challenge.

enrichment.short_title: Gurkha pension, leave pay and family accommodation terms not Article 14 discrimination
key_facts: Seven retired Gurkha soldiers resident in Nepal challenged MoD terms under which Gurkhas receive Indian-based pensions, basic pay only during long leave in Nepal, and family accommodation for only about 25% of married soldiers below warrant-officer rank.

Gurkhas are Nepalese citizens recruited and discharged in Nepal under the 1947 tripartite agreement; a rifleman retiring after 15 years receives about £91 per month pension compared with about £625 for a British soldier after 22 years.
Sullivan J dismissed the claim; the appellants withdrew a concession that pensions could be tailored to Nepalese living costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from Sullivan J's dismissal of a Human Rights Act challenge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no declaratory relief granted on accompanied service.
enrichment.ratio: Gurkha and British soldiers are not in an analogous situation for Article 14 purposes because Gurkhas are recruited, serve and retire in Nepal under distinct tripartite arrangements with earlier pensions, extended home leave and maintained links to Nepal; nationality-based differences in pension, leave pay and accompanied service can therefore be justified without unlawful discrimination.
legal_issues: Whether Gurkha pension and pay terms fall within the ambit of Article 1 Protocol 1 and Article 14
Whether Gurkhas and British soldiers are appropriate comparators under Michalak
Whether the 25% cap on Gurkha married quarters is justified
Whether partial justification for some difference in treatment requires reduction rather than rejection of the policy

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on prison legal visit document policy.

enrichment.short_title: Full Sutton one-day legal document clearance lawful but 'exceptional circumstances' proviso too strict
key_facts: Mr Cannan, a Full Sutton high-security prisoner, challenged a policy requiring written application at least one day before legal visits to hand out or receive legal documents, with late transmission allowed only in 'exceptional circumstances' at an officer's discretion.
Hooper J found the prison's prior practice chaotic and conflicting but upheld the one-day rule as proportionate while accepting concern about the exceptional-circumstances threshold.
After the hearing the prison issued Governor's Order 19/2003 setting out a clearer policy, which the Court of Appeal still found deficient in flexibility.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from Hooper J's dismissal of judicial review.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; no formal relief granted because the impugned policy was superseded; court identified remaining Convention deficiencies in the new Governor's Order.
enrichment.ratio: A high-security prison may require prior clearance of legal documents before visits as a proportionate limit on confidential lawyer-client communication, but any such rule must include a sufficiently flexible proviso so documents that can practicably be cleared on the day of a visit—such as witness statements arriving that morning—are not barred by an 'exceptional circumstances' test or unstructured officer discretion.
legal_issues: Whether the one-day advance clearance requirement infringes Article 6 ECHR
Whether the 'exceptional circumstances' proviso is proportionate
Whether the revised Governor's Order 19/2003 complies with Convention rights

enrichment.short_title: Chagos islanders' strike-out hearing on removal, return and compensation claims
key_facts: Chagos islanders (Ilois/Chagossians) brought group litigation against the Attorney General and BIOT Commissioner seeking compensation, restoration of property rights and declarations concerning their removal from the Chagos archipelago in the 1960s–1970s to facilitate US defence facilities on Diego Garcia.

The population had depended on coconut plantations administered from Mauritius; the UK detached BIOT from Mauritius and implemented a programme of resettlement largely to Mauritius and the Seychelles.

Ouseley J heard defendants' applications to strike out or give summary judgment on multiple causes of action including misfeasance in public office, an alleged tort of unlawful exile, negligence and abuse of process issues tied to 1972 and 1982 settlement agreements.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Group litigation order proceedings; defendants' strike-out and summary judgment applications on preliminary issues, including whether claimants were unlawfully removed or prevented from returning.
enrichment.outcome: Partial strike-out/summary judgment ruling: several heads of claim (including negligence for pure economic loss and broad misfeasance allegations) held to have no reasonable prospects, while a limited personal-injury negligence claim for compulsorily removed islanders was treated as arguable; final paragraphs of the judgment are truncated before all conclusions are recorded.
enrichment.ratio: On the material before the court, claims seeking to impose a broad common-law duty on the Crown to provide transport, employment, housing and welfare for removed islanders, or to recover economic loss in negligence, had no reasonable prospect of success; however, where the state removed a dependent population to an unfamiliar society, it was arguable that a duty existed to take reasonable steps to avoid foreseeable psychiatric and physical injury among those removed.
legal_issues: Whether the claimants were unlawfully removed or prevented from returning to the Chagos islands
Whether misfeasance, unlawful exile and negligence claims disclose any reasonable cause of action
Whether the 1972 and 1982 settlement agreements bar further claims or constitute an abuse of process
Whether signatories to renunciation forms were oppressively exploited

enrichment.short_title: Free car insurance promotions did not reduce VAT on car sales
key_facts: Peugeot and Citroen claimed repayment of output tax totalling about £2.7m and £5.6m respectively on car sales where end-users received free motor insurance paid for by the manufacturers to Orion and Direct Line.

The VAT Tribunal had refused the claims; the manufacturers argued the taxable consideration for each car should be reduced by the insurance premium cost or that a separate exempt insurance-related supply existed.
Sales were made directly to customers or through independent franchised dealers, sometimes involving finance houses.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on points of law from the London VAT Tribunal to the High Court (Chancery Division).
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed and Commissioners' cross-appeal succeeded; taxpayers' application to raise an exempt financial services point refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where a manufacturer promotes car sales by arranging free insurance for the end-user, the transaction is a single taxable supply of a car with ancillary insurance benefits; no part of the price paid by the purchaser is referable to a separate insurance supply, so the manufacturer cannot reduce output tax by the premium paid to the insurer.
legal_issues: Whether free insurance formed part of the consideration for the car supply
Whether Peugeot/Citroen made a separate exempt insurance or financial services supply to dealers or customers
Whether Primback and related ECJ authorities required reduction of the taxable amount
